keyConcepts.title: What the link layer does
keyConcepts.text: Moves a frame across **one link** between adjacent nodes. Services: framing, link access (MAC), reliable delivery (mostly on wireless) and error detection/correction. It's implemented mostly in the **NIC** hardware.

keyConcepts.title: Error detection: parity and CRC
keyConcepts.text: Single parity catches an odd number of bit errors; 2-D parity can **correct** single-bit errors. **CRC**: R = remainder(D·2^r / G) in modulo-2 (XOR) arithmetic. It catches bursts shorter than r + 1 bits.

keyConcepts.title: The multiple access problem
keyConcepts.text: Nodes sharing a broadcast channel collide if they transmit at once. Ideally one node gets rate R, M nodes get R/M each, and the protocol is decentralized and simple.

keyConcepts.title: Three classes of MAC protocols
keyConcepts.text: **Channel partitioning** (TDM, FDM, CDMA), **random access** (ALOHA, CSMA, CSMA/CD) and **taking turns** (polling, token passing).

keyConcepts.title: ALOHA and CSMA/CD efficiency
keyConcepts.text: Slotted ALOHA reaches at most **1/e ≈ 37%**, pure ALOHA **1/(2e) ≈ 18%**. CSMA/CD efficiency = 1/(1 + 5·d_prop/d_trans), with **binary exponential backoff** after collisions.

keyConcepts.title: MAC addresses and ARP
keyConcepts.text: 48-bit, flat, permanent addresses (broadcast FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF). **ARP** maps IP to MAC within a subnet. IP addresses stay the same end to end, while MAC addresses change at every hop.

keyConcepts.title: Ethernet
keyConcepts.text: Frame fields: preamble, destination MAC, source MAC, type, data (46–1,500 bytes) and CRC. Connectionless and unreliable. Switched full-duplex Ethernet has **no collisions**.

keyConcepts.title: Switches
keyConcepts.text: Self-learning (record each source MAC and its port), then **flood, filter or forward**. They're plug-and-play and eliminate collisions, but are limited to a spanning tree and vulnerable to broadcast storms.

keyConcepts.title: VLANs
keyConcepts.text: One physical switch acts as several isolated LANs (broadcast domains). Trunk ports carry several VLANs using **802.1Q tags**, and a router connects VLANs.

keyConcepts.title: MPLS and data centers
keyConcepts.text: MPLS forwards on short labels, enabling traffic engineering, fast restoration and VPNs. Data centers use racks with TOR switches, load balancers and highly connected **Clos** topologies.

keyConcepts.title: A day in the life of a web request
keyConcepts.text: DHCP → ARP → DNS → intra- and inter-domain routing (OSPF, BGP) → TCP handshake → HTTP GET and response. Every layer works together.

flashcards.back: Node: any device running a link-layer protocol (host, router, switch, AP). Link: the channel connecting adjacent nodes.
The link-layer packet: a datagram encapsulated with link-layer header fields and a trailer.

flashcards.front: Where is the link layer implemented?
flashcards.back: Mostly in the network adapter (NIC) hardware, partly in software on the host.
It detects only an odd number of bit errors; an even number of flipped bits goes unnoticed.
Row and column parity bits. It can detect and correct a single-bit error, and detect any two-bit error.
The receiver detects AND corrects errors without asking for a retransmission.
**R = remainder( D·2^r ÷ G )** using modulo-2 (XOR) division, where G is the (r+1)-bit generator.
It detects all burst errors shorter than r + 1 bits and any odd number of bit errors.
Point-to-point: one sender and one receiver. Broadcast: many nodes share one channel, and every node receives each frame.
A node is limited to R/N even when it's the only node with data to send.
**1/e ≈ 0.37**: at best, 37% of slots carry successful transmissions.
**1/(2e) ≈ 0.18**, half of slotted ALOHA, because its collision window is twice as long.

flashcards.front: Why do collisions still happen with carrier sensing?
flashcards.back: Propagation delay: a node may start sending before it hears that another node already began.
Listen before sending; if a collision is detected while sending, abort immediately, then back off for a random time.
After the n-th collision, choose K from {0, 1, …, 2^n − 1} and wait K × 512 bit times.
**1 / (1 + 5·d_prop/d_trans)**. It approaches 1 as d_prop → 0 or as d_trans → ∞.
Polling delay, and the master node is a single point of failure.
If one node fails (or loses the token), the whole channel can crash.

MAC is like a social security number (flat, never changes). IP is like a postal address (hierarchical, changes when you move).
Finds the MAC address for an IP address on the same subnet: a broadcast query, then a unicast reply.

flashcards.front: Sending to another subnet: which MAC goes in the frame?
flashcards.back: The MAC address of the first-hop router's interface, not the final destination's.
Preamble (8), destination MAC (6), source MAC (6), type (2), data (46–1,500), CRC (4).
1,500 bytes of data.
No. It's connectionless and unreliable: a frame that fails the CRC is just discarded, with no ACK or NAK.
A hub is a layer-1 repeater that sends bits out every port (collisions possible). A switch is a layer-2 store-and-forward device (no collisions).
Record (source MAC, incoming interface, time) for each frame; delete entries after an aging time.
Flood the frame out every interface except the one it arrived on.

flashcards.front: Switch: destination on the same interface it arrived on
flashcards.back: Filter: discard the frame.
An attacker floods the switch with bogus source MACs, filling the table so the switch broadcasts frames, which lets the attacker sniff them.
Switches are plug-and-play and fast, but limited to a spanning tree and exposed to broadcast storms. Routers use hierarchical addresses, take the best paths and block broadcast storms.
A trunk port carries frames for all VLANs; an 802.1Q 4-byte tag (with a 12-bit VLAN ID) says which VLAN each frame belongs to.
A label between the layer-2 and IP headers, enabling traffic engineering, fast restoration and VPNs.
The Top of Rack switch connecting the 20–40 hosts (blades) in a data center rack.

flashcards.front: Why are data center load balancers called layer-4 switches?
flashcards.back: They decide using the destination port (layer 4) as well as the IP address, and spread requests across servers.
Every tier-1 switch connects to every tier-2 switch, giving high host-to-host capacity and many disjoint paths.

quiz.q: Which error-detection method can also CORRECT a single-bit error?
quiz.explain: The row and column with bad parity pinpoint the flipped bit, so it can be corrected.

quiz.q: D = 101110, G = 1001 (r = 3). What is the CRC R?
quiz.explain: Divide 101110000 by 1001 using XOR. The remainder is 011, so the sender transmits 101110011.

quiz.q: What is the maximum efficiency of slotted ALOHA?
quiz.explain: With many active nodes and the best p, at most 1/e ≈ 37% of slots succeed.

quiz.q: Why can collisions still occur in CSMA?
options: Propagation delay: a node may not yet hear another node's transmission
quiz.explain: The signal takes time to travel, so two nodes can both sense an idle channel and transmit.

quiz.q: After the 3rd collision of a frame, binary exponential backoff picks K from which set?
quiz.explain: K is chosen from {0, …, 2^n − 1}; with n = 3, that's {0, …, 7}.

quiz.q: Which protocol class uses a master node to invite others to transmit?
quiz.explain: In polling, the master polls each node in turn. Its weaknesses are polling delay and a single point of failure.

quiz.q: How long is a MAC address?
quiz.explain: MAC addresses are 6 bytes (48 bits); 32 bits is IPv4 and 128 bits is IPv6.

options: Finds the MAC address for an IP address on the same subnet
Finds the IP address for a hostname
quiz.explain: ARP broadcasts a query; the interface with that IP replies with its MAC address. (DNS maps names to IPs; DHCP assigns IPs.)

quiz.q: Host A sends a datagram to host B on a different subnet. What destination MAC address does A use in the frame?
options: The MAC of A's first-hop router interface
quiz.explain: Frames only travel one link. The router then builds a new frame for the next link, while the IP addresses stay the same.

quiz.q: What does an Ethernet adapter do with a frame that fails its CRC check?
quiz.explain: Ethernet is unreliable; higher layers like TCP recover any missing data.

quiz.q: A switch receives a frame whose destination MAC isn't in its table. What does it do?
options: Floods it out all interfaces except the incoming one
quiz.explain: Flooding ensures the frame reaches its destination, and the reply will teach the switch where that host is.

quiz.q: Why are there no collisions in a modern switched, full-duplex Ethernet?
options: Each link connects one host to a switch port, which buffers and sends one frame at a time
quiz.explain: With point-to-point full-duplex links to a buffering switch, no two nodes share a channel, so no MAC protocol is needed.

quiz.q: What does a VLAN trunk port do?
options: Carries frames for all VLANs between switches, using 802.1Q tags
Connects a VLAN to the Internet
quiz.explain: The 4-byte 802.1Q tag records which VLAN each frame belongs to as it crosses the trunk.

quiz.q: Which is a main advantage of MPLS?
options: Traffic engineering: sending traffic on paths regular IP routing wouldn't choose
quiz.explain: MPLS also enables fast restoration and VPNs.

quiz.q: In 'a day in the life of a web request', what does the laptop do right after getting an IP address from DHCP and before sending the DNS query?
options: Uses ARP to find the gateway router's MAC address
Opens a TCP connection to Google
quiz.explain: The DNS query must go in a frame to the gateway router, so the laptop first needs that router's MAC address.
